\section[convertirse]{convertirse — to become, to turn into}

\label{lesson:ES-C572-convertirse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the origin, then the Spanish for the development.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: convertirse}
\textbf{convertirse} — \textquotedblleft{}to become, to turn into\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El pueblo se convirtió en una ciudad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The village turned into a city.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Convertirse en} + noun. Stem change: \emph{se convierte}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{convertirse} comes from Latin \emph{convertere} 'to turn around, to change' (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{con-} and \emph{vertere} 'to turn'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{convertirse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{convertirse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{convertirse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the origin, then the Spanish for the development, then say \emph{convertirse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does convertirse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To become, to turn into\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[transformar]{transformar — to transform}

\label{lesson:ES-C572-transformar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the development, then the Spanish for to become.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: transformar}
\textbf{transformar} — \textquotedblleft{}to transform\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Transformaron la fábrica en un museo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They turned the factory into a museum.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{transformar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{trānsfōrmāre} 'to change in shape' (EtymDB), built on \emph{trāns} 'across' and \emph{forma} 'shape'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{transformar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{transformar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{transformar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the development, then the Spanish for to become, then say \emph{transformar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does transformar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To transform\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[evolucionar]{evolucionar — to evolve, to progress}

\label{lesson:ES-C572-evolucionar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to become, then the Spanish for to transform.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: evolucionar}
\textbf{evolucionar} — \textquotedblleft{}to evolve, to progress\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El paciente evoluciona bien.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The patient is progressing well.}
\end{quote}

Used for patients, situations and species.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{evolucionar} is built on \emph{evolución}, from Latin \emph{ēvolūtiō} 'an unrolling' (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{ēvolvere}, built on \emph{volvere} 'to roll'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{evolucionar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{evolucionar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{evolucionar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to become, then the Spanish for to transform, then say \emph{evolucionar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does evolucionar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To evolve, to progress\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[desarrollar]{desarrollar — to develop}

\label{lesson:ES-C572-desarrollar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to transform, then the Spanish for to evolve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desarrollar}
\textbf{desarrollar} — \textquotedblleft{}to develop\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La empresa desarrolló un coche nuevo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The company developed a new car.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Desarrollarse} is to take place or to develop: \emph{La historia se desarrolla en Lima.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desarrollar} is built on \emph{arrollar} 'to roll up' with \emph{des-} 'un-'. \emph{Arrollar} comes from \emph{rollo}, usually traced to Latin \emph{rotulus} 'a little wheel', built on \emph{rota} 'wheel'. To develop is to unroll.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desarrollar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desarrollar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{desarrollar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to transform, then the Spanish for to evolve, then say \emph{desarrollar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does desarrollar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To develop\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[superar]{superar — to overcome, to get over; to beat}

\label{lesson:ES-C572-superar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to evolve, then the Spanish for to develop.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: superar}
\textbf{superar} — \textquotedblleft{}to overcome, to get over; to beat\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Le costó mucho superar la muerte de su padre.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It was very hard for him to get over his father's death.}
\end{quote}

It also means to exceed: \emph{superar un récord}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{superar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{superāre} 'to go over, to rise above' (EtymDB), built on \emph{super} 'over'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{superar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{superar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{superar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to evolve, then the Spanish for to develop, then say \emph{superar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does superar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To overcome, to get over; to beat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
